title: The Franciscan crown
hookLine: a seven-decade rosary of Mary's joys

lines: NO MORE FLOWERS IN THE FRIARY.
cards: A young man has a habit. Every so often he picks wildflowers, weaves them into a little crown, and sets it on the head of a statue of Mary.
Then he joins the Franciscans, and in the friary there's no time for flower-picking. The crowns stop. He's heartbroken, so much so, the story goes, that he thinks about leaving.
Then, as he prays, Mary appears to him. Don't be sad, she tells him. Instead of flowers that wither, weave me a crown that won't: say your prayers in honor of seven joys of my life.
That, tradition says, is how a new kind of rosary began.

teach.b: This path met the rosary's beads and decades long ago. The Franciscan crown, sometimes called the Seraphic rosary, has seven decades instead of five. Each decade is an Our Father and ten Hail Marys, and each holds a joy.
The first is the Annunciation, when the angel Gabriel greets Mary, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women."
The second is the Visitation, Mary hurrying to her cousin Elizabeth and the child leaping in Elizabeth's womb. The third, the birth of Jesus. The fourth, the wise men coming to adore him.
The fifth, finding the boy Jesus in the Temple after three days of searching.
Those five come straight from Luke and Matthew.
The last two come from the Church's tradition. The sixth is the risen Jesus appearing to his mother, a meeting the Gospels don't describe but tradition holds.
The seventh is Mary's Assumption into heaven and her crowning as queen. The usual rosary's mysteries take in sorrows as well as joys and glories.

teach.h: A ROSARY THAT STAYS WITH JOY.
teach.b: This one stays with joy. It isn't that Franciscans deny sorrow; tradition says Francis bore the wounds of Christ in his own body.
But the family that told of perfect joy at a locked gate also made a rosary of pure gladness, and gave it to Mary as a crown. And joy, here, isn't a mood.
It's a list of things that happened: a greeting, a visit, a birth, a homecoming, a reunion. Each bead is a reason.

how: Franciscans and other Catholics pray the Franciscan crown on a seven-decade rosary, meditating on the seven joys of Mary, one joy for each decade.

games.q: you're the young friar. you used to crown Mary's statue with flowers, but in the friary there's no time. what does the story say happens?
o: you leave the friary to keep your custom.
Mary tells you to weave a crown of prayers for her seven joys.
you give up the custom and forget it.
games.why: tradition says Mary appeared and asked for a crown that wouldn't wither: prayers in honor of her seven joys.

practice: If you pray the rosary, say seven Hail Marys, one for each of Mary's joys: the greeting, the visit, the birth, the wise men, the boy found, the risen son, the crown.
If you don't, count seven joys from your own life on your fingers: a phone call that came, a child born, a reunion. Go slowly, and let each one be a bead.

wordCard.voice: The Franciscan crown. A seven-decade rosary, a garland of Hail Marys woven around seven joys of Mary. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: joy, gladness; the seven joys are the septem gaudia.

carryVoice: Your line: seven joys. A crown of prayers that won't wither, the story says. Until tomorrow.
